title: Databases after Microservices: PostgreSQL or MongoDB in a Domain‑Driven Design?
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
When an enterprise chooses a database for new workloads—whether for a new application or to modernize a legacy system—the next question is often: PostgreSQL or MongoDB. PostgreSQL is one of the most popular SQL databases among developers, while MongoDB is the most popular NoSQL database. Both are general-purpose and suitable for OLTP and complex transactional systems of record. However, this doesn’t mean you must choose a single database technology for the entire organization. Thanks to cloud automation—on-premises or via managed services—along with AI-assisted development and multi-dialect frameworks, it’s not difficult to adopt multiple database technologies. This offers a manageable compromise between single‑vendor database strategies of the pre‑cloud era and the purpose-built database sprawl that followed the rise of cloud platforms.

It’s about architecture and responsibility, more than features

Both databases can handle similar categories of data and workloads, including ACID transactions, text and vector search, time-series data, and spatial data, and support various deployment options.

  • PostgreSQL is valued for its extensibility, diverse extensions and forks, and large open-source ecosystem, supported by different companies and managed services.
  • MongoDB offers built-in features that provide the same capabilities in a single data platform, with support and managed services from a single company across multiple clouds.

Comparing features goes beyond a simple checklist and includes differences in performance, operational complexity, and total cost of ownership. Since this analysis varies based on your specific situation, there is no straightforward decision tree. The primary factor in choosing between databases is how responsibilities are assigned to application developers and how each data platform fits into your architecture—either as a centralized system of record or as part of a bounded-context-focused, microservices-based structure.

The shift introduced by microservices is about responsibility allocation rather than technology itself. To determine the right database, it’s essential to understand what modern architectures optimize for, including how Domain-Driven Design (DDD), CQRS, and event-driven systems influence the role of databases.

What users actually want: one truth and fast change

Throughout the evolution of technology, user expectations have remained largely the same:

  • A single, authoritative view of the business, instead of conflicting sources of truth
  • A robust, meaningful data model that accurately reflects business concepts
  • Guarantees of durability, correctness, and consistency, even in the presence of failures
  • Predictable system behavior under load, independent of timing or concurrency concerns

What has changed is the way we build systems:

  • Small, autonomous teams with end-to-end bounded context ownership
  • Independent deployments that avoid global synchronization across teams
  • Rapid iteration cycles that support continuous refinement of the domain model and frequent delivery of new features
  • Starting small and moving fast with a minimum viable product and tight feedback loops
  • Operational resilience and release without downtime

For decades, enterprises have known how to optimize for correctness in centralized systems. Today, they are still learning how to preserve that same level of correctness while moving quickly in distributed, domain-driven architectures.

SQL: one system, one truth

Traditional enterprise systems were built around a simple assumption: the database is the system. Relational databases became the central authority: One database, a schema shared by multiple applications, one transaction manager, and a single service that provides all operations without physical segregation of responsibility:

  • DDL (data definition language) to modify the schema shared by all applications
  • DML to manipulate data with generic CRUD (create, read, update, delete) commands and queries in a stateful session with multiple calls to the database

Even with RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) in place, a traditional SQL database exposes a single logical service for all data and metadata operations across all bounded contexts, applications, and users, the SQL endpoint. One premise of relational databases is to allow access for non-programmer users, not just applications, and that's why they encourage placing all access control, data integrity, and business logic in the database so it cannot be bypassed by a manual SQL command line connected to production. This explains why SQL databases traditionally provide:

  • A normalized relational model independent of the business domains, and that avoids update anomalies when direct update statements are executed without knowing the full schema and going through a validated application
  • A maximum of integrity constraints, like referential integrity (foreign keys), to guarantee the correctness of the normalized table relationships, and SQL assertions or triggers to implement more complex business rules
  • Stored procedures to encapsulate all business logic so that arbitrary commands that bypass the application cannot violate the business invariants, and allow a business transaction to be a single autocommit call to the database rather than an interactive dialogue that holds locks across network calls and context switches.

This model is powerful. It excels at strong consistency and data integrity, even with non-trusted users or applications. But it comes with a cost: every change to the schema or business rules requires coordination between multiple application development teams and the database administrator (DBA). Schemas are shared, deployments are synchronized and scheduled during maintenance windows, and evolution may slow as systems grow.

NoSQL: speed first, structure later

As organizations aimed to move more quickly, they adopted service-oriented architecture, formed smaller teams, and enabled independent deployment. Early NoSQL systems focused on eventual consistency, flexible schemas, and minimal coordination. This approach improved speed but often led to weak or implicit data models, inconsistent interpretations of similar concepts, fragile integrations, and analytics challenges. While these systems became faster, the overall information system became more fragmented.

This NoSQL approach has encouraged reconsideration of the traditional monolithic model. Eventual consistency introduced the idea that an event-driven architecture can enhance scalability, benefiting both development—by enabling multiple teams to work simultaneously without delays—and deployment—by minimizing the impact of failures and allowing individual service scalability. Additionally, enterprises experienced a shift: database administrators no longer exclusively controlled company data, as developers gained the freedom to build independently and only involve operations during production.

The convergence: domain‑driven organizations

Modern architecture is not a rejection of modeling or consistency. It is a redistribution of responsibility. Domain‑Driven Design provides the structure needed to reconcile speed with correctness—especially when reasoning about databases. As it decouples database applications into bounded contexts, it uses multiple databases rather than a single one, but this must be done without breaking data consistency. Three DDD concepts directly shape persistence decisions:

  • Aggregates, where consistency is non‑negotiable. An aggregate defines a transactional boundary where all invariants must be maintained, updates are atomic, and strong consistency is required. They often involve ownership relationships, typically one‑to‑many, within a consistency boundary, which leads SQL databases to split data across multiple tables and to perform multi-statement transactions. In contrast, document databases preserve aggregate atomicity by embedding strong relationships directly within the document API and in storage caches and persistent storage.
  • Bounded contexts, where the schema belongs to the application. A bounded context defines a ubiquitous language and a domain model that evolves as a coherent unit. It groups together concepts that change for the same reasons and at a similar pace: business rules, schema structure, cardinalities, relationships, and object lifecycles. SQL databases provide a logical model, with views and stored procedures to name entities, attributes, and transactions in the domain's ubiquitous language, while sharing a physical model with others. Document databases are commonly deployed per bounded context, and while they trust the application for the schema and the business logic invariants, they allow enforcing parts of the schema in the database as the model stabilizes, with indexes (which already encode schema by naming fields) and additional validation rules (raising errors or logging warnings with per-document schema validation). The schema declared in the database evolves with the bounded context, not ahead of it.
  • Domains, where bounded contexts integrate with each other. Across bounded contexts, terminology and models vary, and maintaining consistency depends on the context. Sharing tables or schemas, as in traditional monolithic approaches, tends to let one bounded context overpower the others. Modern systems typically employ separate databases for each bounded context and integrate through application APIs rather than sharing data directly in the database. They also prioritize translating schemas over reusing them.

In a document database like MongoDB, aggregates are often mapped to a single document when the consistency boundary allows it: one write, one index lookup, no joins, no foreign-key cascades, no ORM proxies, no lazy-loading surprises. The persistence model finally aligns with the domain model instead of fighting it. Schema validation in MongoDB is optional and evolves with the domain model. It never requires you to migrate the entire system before deploying a new feature. MongoDB databases lack a central catalog and are lightweight, so having one database per domain doesn't increase operational complexity and can even offer greater flexibility in choosing deployment topology, replication factor, and read and write concerns per domain or service.

Relationships in relational databases vs. the domain's model associations

Relational databases are often called “better at relationships”, but those relationships are defined at the data level rather than the domain‑semantic level. The strong ties are only between attributes sharing the same key, defining a relation (a table in SQL). Between tables, relationships are defined by business values (foreign keys in SQL) rather than pointers (though most databases deviate from this and introduce surrogate keys to avoid relying on business values) or by co-location in arrays or objects. In SQL databases, relationships are typically implemented using foreign keys to define one-to-many relationships, and they do not encode expected cardinality (whether there are few or millions in the "many" side), lifecycle intent (except for some cascading foreign key options), or navigation direction (except when creating optimal indexes). In a relational model, the characteristics of a relationship (such as association, aggregation, composition, and inheritance) are lost because they are domain-specific.

DDD reframes the question of relationships:

  • Inside an aggregate, there is strong ownership, strong consistency, and a single transactional boundary. All invariants are enforced atomically in the application and, optionally, gradually with schema validation in the database.
  • Across aggregates within a bounded context, relationships are expressed through identity‑based references. Invariants do not cascade across aggregate boundaries, and consistency is enforced locally.
  • Across bounded contexts, there is no shared persistence model or implicit coupling. Coordination happens through explicit contracts and domain events, with consistency achieved asynchronously.

Across bounded contexts, communication occurs through events rather than through shared tables or schemas. Each bounded context owns its data model and enforces its own invariants. Coordination across bounded contexts is therefore asynchronous and explicit. This relies on well‑known consistency patterns such as:

  • Outbox pattern: domain state changes and outgoing events are recorded atomically in the same transaction, ensuring events are never lost or published without the corresponding state change.
  • Saga (choreography): long‑running business processes are coordinated through a sequence of domain events, with each bounded context reacting independently and applying compensating actions when needed, rather than relying on distributed transactions.
  • Event correlation: business identifiers are used to relate events belonging to the same business process across bounded contexts, enabling traceability and reconciliation without tight coupling.
  • Deferred publication: events are visible to other bounded contexts only after the transaction is complete, preventing consumers from seeing intermediate or inconsistent states.
  • Idempotent consumers: event handlers are designed to tolerate duplicates and replays, making the system resilient to retries and at‑least‑once delivery semantics.
  • Versioned event contracts: events are treated as stable integration contracts that evolve through versioning rather than breaking changes, allowing bounded contexts to evolve independently.

Consistency is not weaker—it is explicit, observable, and aligned with business workflows rather than technical transactions.

Within a bounded context, aggregates may also communicate through domain events—either synchronously in‑process or asynchronously—but without sharing transactional boundaries. Each aggregate remains responsible for enforcing its own invariants.

Multitenancy: a domain problem, not a database feature

In centralized SQL systems, multitenancy is often achieved through shared schemas, tenant-identifier columns, row-level security (RLS), or virtual private databases (VPDs). These methods provide logical separation within a single database and are well-suited to database-centric architectures in which the database serves as a shared system of record. As multiple applications, with different owners, can access the database, the only universally trusted method to isolate tenants must reside in the database.

However, from a Domain‑Driven Design (DDD) perspective, multitenancy is not primarily a filtering problem—it is often a bounded context and ownership problem. Tenants often differ in fundamental ways, including geographic location and data residency requirements, legal and regulatory constraints, tax rules and accounting policies, and operational and availability needs. Row‑level security does not address these concerns. While it hides rows from queries, it does not provide physical isolation of data, independent backup and restore, regional or jurisdictional separation, reduced blast radius during incidents, or schema changes.

As soon as these requirements appear, designs tend to evolve toward database‑per‑tenant, collection‑per‑tenant, or database‑per‑region models. This shift highlights a key difference between SQL‑centric and domain‑centric architectures. In SQL systems, sharing a schema across databases means synchronizing DDL changes, managing migration scripts, and coordinating schema evolution. That overhead has historically pushed architects toward shared databases with row‑level security (RLS). In a domain‑driven architecture, the schema is defined and enforced by the application as part of the domain model. The database is not the primary authority for schema evolution, so you don’t need tightly coordinated migrations across many databases. Multiple databases with the same logical schema are not an inconsistency—they follow naturally from bounded context ownership.

This architectural perspective explains why native row-level security hasn't been a primary focus for MongoDB. MongoDB users assume:

  • access through a trusted, reviewed application code
  • isolation through ownership rather than row filtering
  • security boundaries defined at the application and deployment level

This example shows that when switching from a relational to a document database, it's not wise to map features directly one-to-one. Instead, focus on understanding the core needs behind relational features and modify them based on domain-driven design principles and the traits of a document database. If you don't trust your developers or applications to access the database, it's safer to stick with a monolithic relational database and keep all business logic inside it, even if this slows development—but that's acceptable for legacy applications that don’t need modernization. In a domain-driven design architecture, consider the entire application, not just the database, when mapping features between database technologies.

CQRS as a modeling pattern (not just read replicas)

In Domain‑Driven Design, Command–Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) is not just an infrastructure optimization but a modeling and responsibility‑allocation pattern. A bounded context owns its data through aggregates, each with a single owner responsible for enforcing invariants. CQRS clarifies this by splitting responsibilities into:

  • Command services that modify state and enforce business rules
  • Query services that expose data optimized for reading and navigation

The command side is authoritative, and the query side is derived. This allows each side to evolve independently while maintaining strong consistency where it matters most: within the aggregate.

Database administrators sometimes treat CQRS as a deployment pattern. Simply adding read replicas to a monolithic database does not make it CQRS. Replicas share the same data model, schema, and indexes, and still add load to the primary, which must keep them synchronized. Even if reads move off the primary, the command side still bears schema coupling and index maintenance for the read services. This approach scales within a single shared model instead of clearly splitting responsibilities, and it is usually limited unless combined with sharding: when replicas store identical data, load balancing can increase CPU capacity but not improve storage or memory capacity.

CQRS is about different models for different purposes, not just the same model on different nodes.

Within a bounded context, CQRS allows read models to diverge from write models while remaining consistent with domain-specific rules. MongoDB makes this separation natural: read‑oriented workloads, such as text or vector search, can use indexes maintained asynchronously via change streams, decoupled from the write-transaction path. This reduces coupling between command and query concerns, letting read models evolve independently while preserving strong consistency for aggregate updates. The same change data capture is available to the application for managing its own event sourcing, integrated with the built-in replication and resilience to failure.

Across bounded contexts, CQRS extends naturally to event‑driven integration:

  • Command models emit domain events
  • Other domains build read models from those events
  • No shared tables or schemas
  • No cross‑domain transactions

CQRS doesn't dilute consistency. It simply separates the operational truth from the read-optimized projections.

Choosing the right database based on the bounded context and responsibility

The question “PostgreSQL or MongoDB?” is often asked too early. In a domain‑driven architecture, the more useful question is: What responsibility does this bounded context have, and how does it evolve?

Analytics: a bounded context beyond CQRS.

Analytics is often conflated with CQRS read models, but it is a distinct bounded context with different goals. Analytics does not primarily serve application queries. It answers questions such as: trends over time, aggregations and correlations, forecasting, and exploratory analysis. Analytics consumes events, operational data extracts, or snapshots and builds projections, but unlike CQRS read models, it is not concerned with enforcing business invariants or serving transactional workflows.

This bounded context:

  • tolerates eventual consistency
  • favors append‑only and denormalized data
  • optimizes for scans and aggregations rather than point updates

When analytics becomes a first‑class concern, neither MongoDB nor PostgreSQL is an ideal fit. Columnar databases such as ClickHouse or DuckDB are better suited, and data often belongs in object storage rather than block storage.

Forcing analytics into an OLTP database:

  • pollutes transactional models
  • introduces indexes irrelevant to command workloads
  • slows down writes
  • couples unrelated concerns

DDD makes this separation explicit by treating analytics as its own bounded context. This is different from analytical queries on operational databases, which MongoDB supports through consistent secondary indexes, or text and vector search indexes on dedicated nodes, and aggregation framework pipelines.

Transactional: PostgreSQL and MongoDB as complementary choices

In a transactional bounded context, PostgreSQL (with extensions) and MongoDB largely overlap in their data types and workloads. Both can support:

  • ACID transactions
  • Rich indexing strategies
  • Text and vector search
  • Time‑series and spatial data
  • High availability and multiple deployment models

The distinction is not about capability, but about how bounded context logic, schema, and responsibility are expressed.

PostgreSQL: Database-centric with relational normalization

PostgreSQL feels most natural when your domain model requires strict, database-level schema enforcement and strong relational normalization shared across multiple bounded contexts. It is the first choice for centralized, database-first architectures. This makes PostgreSQL an excellent fit for:

  • Database‑centric architectures where the database remains the primary authority, especially when accessed by un-trusted applications or tenants.
  • Teams that rely heavily on SQL for both data access and business logic, and who are proficient in tuning object-relational mapping (avoid lazy N+1 that hits latency, and avoid eager fetching that hits throughput).
  • Legacy systems that are split into bounded contexts without deep modernization, where PL/SQL was translated to PL/pgSQL in a lift and shift from proprietary to open-source, without reconsidering the service responsibilities.

In these contexts, PostgreSQL offers continuity, power, and maturity. The various forks and managed services offer a range of high availability features not available in vanilla PostgreSQL.

MongoDB: Application-centric for aggregate-oriented agility

MongoDB tends to be more comfortable when the bounded context is modeled primarily around aggregates and fast-paced iteration. Because the schema is governed by the application, it removes the friction of object-relational mapping (ORM) and aligns perfectly with a code-first approach. MongoDB shines for:

  • Bounded contexts that are modeled tightly around self-contained aggregates, optimizing for single-document atomic writes.
  • Domains where schema evolution is frequent, expected, and driven by application deployments rather than coordinated database migrations.
  • Architectures where business logic lives strictly in the application code, expressed in the ubiquitous language rather than translated to normalized constraints and stored procedures.
  • Services that own their data entirely and integrate across boundaries explicitly through events.

For teams embracing DDD, CQRS, and event-driven architectures, MongoDB reduces friction by aligning persistence directly with bounded context ownership and aggregate boundaries, helping organizations modernize without the operational weight of a centralized monolith.

A composition, not a compromise

Both SQL and NoSQL have evolved significantly in features, but their core distinction remains: SQL emphasizes normalization and abstraction, while NoSQL focuses on data locality and placing responsibility within the bounded context. In a domain-driven architecture, PostgreSQL and MongoDB can work together effectively, since different bounded contexts can—and often should—make different choices:

  • OLTP bounded contexts optimized for agility and evolution, easier without additional object-relational mapping (ORM)
  • Legacy bounded contexts with stable business logic in SQL and PL/SQL
  • Analytics bounded contexts optimized for large‑scale analysis

DDD does not mandate a single database. It enables intentional, bounded-context‑aligned choices.

Conclusion: the achievable middle ground with DDD

Domain‑Driven Design enables something that was historically difficult: using different databases for different bounded contexts and workloads—intentionally. Enterprises once oscillated between two extremes: a single database for the entire enterprise or a proliferation of specialized databases for every use case. Today, a pragmatic middle ground is achievable: a small set of general‑purpose databases, each aligned with a bounded context and its responsibilities. For example:

  • PostgreSQL for a centralized database shared by different applications
  • MongoDB for OLTP that requires agility, availability, and scalability
  • ClickHouse or DuckDB for analytics on large volumes of historical data

Here is a summary of the strengths of PostgreSQL and MongoDB for each DDD concept:

1. The Aggregate (Consistency Boundary)

  • PostgreSQL: Handles consistency via multi-table relationships and multi-statement transactions.
  • MongoDB: Optimizes for "data locality," keeping the aggregate within a single document to enable atomic, high-performance writes.

2. The Bounded Context (Ownership)

  • PostgreSQL: Often favors a shared schema approach with views and stored procedures acting as the interface.
  • MongoDB: Encourages each service to own its own schema, allowing teams to deploy independently without global synchronization.

3. Cross-Domain Integration

  • PostgreSQL: Traditionally relies on foreign keys and shared tables. Scales vertically to handle growth.
  • MongoDB: Favors event-driven integration and explicit contracts. Scales horizontally to handle elasticity and resilience.

4. Schema Evolution

  • PostgreSQL: Requires coordinated DDL migrations to keep business rules in sync across the database.
  • MongoDB: Supports gradual, application-driven changes. You trust the developers and add validation in the database as the domain stabilizes, not before.

With advances in cloud automation and AI-assisted development, managing multiple databases has become safer and more reliable. The main challenge is no longer having many databases, but avoiding a single database that tries to serve too many conflicting roles. As development accelerates, organizations gain by adopting domain-driven design.

Each bounded context can evolve its database independently, without the constant cross-team coordination a single, centralized source of truth requires. In this context, PostgreSQL is a natural fit for SQL-centric, database-first architectures, while MongoDB better serves application-first, aggregate-oriented domains that need to evolve quickly.
